analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, 24.7% of firms in Health care and social assistance (NAICS 62) answered yes to whether they had used AI in the last two weeks, up from 24.0% in the prior period. The question was first asked in September 2023. That is the only measured adoption figure in this material, and it covers the whole sector, from large hospital systems to small social assistance providers, so it should be read as a sector-wide floor rather than a picture of clinical deployment specifically.

The material describes the sector's AI work as concentrating in imaging diagnostics, clinical documentation, and drug discovery. The National Institutes of Health frames its role as making biomedical data findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable, or FAIR, and as making that data usable with AI and machine learning applications, drawing on electronic health record data, omics data, imaging data, and disease-specific data. The World Health Organization describes the promise of these technologies in similar terms, naming diagnosis, treatment, health research and drug development, and government public health functions including surveillance and outbreak response.

Quality measurement is where the sources are most concrete. OpenAI's HealthBench was built in partnership with 262 physicians who have practiced in 60 countries and contains 5,000 realistic health conversations, each with a physician-created rubric, totaling 48,562 unique rubric criteria, with responses graded by a model-based grader. OpenAI reports that o3 outperforms other models including Claude 3.7 Sonnet and Gemini 2.5 Pro, that its frontier models improved by 28% on HealthBench in recent months, and that GPT-4.1 nano outperforms August 2024's GPT-4o despite being 25x cheaper. It also reports that its most recent models show substantially improved worst-of-n performance while significant room for further gains remains, and it holds back 1,000 harder examples as HealthBench Hard. Artificial Analysis offers a vendor-neutral alternative, benchmarking models across quality, price, output speed and latency, and measuring how much of a model's accuracy a given provider endpoint preserves.

On vendors and money, KLAS Research collects its rankings directly from people using healthcare IT, including executives, physicians, nurses, IT professionals, and administrators, and its annual Best in KLAS report recognizes software and services companies that help organizations accomplish the Quadruple Aim. KLAS has published this research since 1996 and sells memberships to vendors, payers, investors, government agencies, and associations. Rock Health publishes widely cited research on digital health funding, which is the standard record of where capital in this space lands, though the excerpt available here does not give figures.

The regulatory and ethical posture is set out most fully by the World Health Organization, whose guidance on the ethics and governance of AI for health is the product of eighteen months of deliberation among experts in ethics, digital technology, law, and human rights, along with Ministries of Health. It identifies ethical challenges and risks, sets out six consensus principles to ensure AI works to the public benefit of all countries, and recommends governance that holds public and private sector stakeholders accountable to healthcare workers and to the communities affected. The National Institutes of Health points to policies, guidelines, and best practices that investigators should consider. OpenAI notes that in health a single unsafe or incorrect answer can outweigh the benefit of many good ones.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a few practical conclusions. Adoption is real but not dominant, at 24.7% of firms per the Census Bureau. Independent evaluation exists and is worth using before clinical deployment, whether through HealthBench's physician-written rubrics or Artificial Analysis's vendor-neutral comparisons. Provider experience is a separate signal from benchmark scores, which is what KLAS collects. And the governance expectations from the World Health Organization are framed as applying to public and private sector stakeholders alike, not only to model developers.

https://klasresearch.com/.brief: KLAS Research is a community that brings together healthcare leaders, IT professionals, and vendors to share candid provider feedback and collaborate on best practices. The organization gathers insights directly from thousands of healthcare professionals, executives, physicians, nurses, IT staff, and administrators, who use IT solutions and services, and uses that feedback to produce market reports and live data. Its annual Best in KLAS report ranks software and services companies that help healthcare organizations achieve the Quadruple Aim, based on year-long feedback from provider and payer professionals. Since 1996, KLAS has aimed to improve healthcare by amplifying provider and payer voices and expanding its research scope to meet evolving technology needs.

https://artificialanalysis.ai/.brief: Artificial Analysis presents independent benchmarks for AI models and API hosting providers, comparing quality, price, output speed, and latency. The page explains that its AA-AnalystAgent benchmark measures how reliably a model answers quantitative analysis questions correctly across five independent attempts, and that evaluation costs are calculated from token prices and usage. It also notes that provider endpoint scores indicate how much of a model’s accuracy is preserved, with lower scores reflecting losses from quantization, sampling defaults, or other endpoint-side configuration.

https://rockhealth.com/insights/.brief: The page says it publishes perspectives on trends shaping the future of healthcare. It notes that its work is at the forefront of digital health. Readers are invited to browse its research on digital health funding and special topics in the healthcare industry. The research is described as “widely-cited.”

https://openai.com/index/healthbench/.brief: HealthBench is a new benchmark for AI in healthcare that evaluates models in realistic scenarios, built with input from 262 physicians across 60 countries. It contains 5,000 “realistic health conversations,” each graded by a physician-written rubric with 48,562 unique criteria, and responses are scored by a GPT-4.1 grader. OpenAI reports that its frontier models, such as o3, have outperformed others and improved by 28% on HealthBench, while a small GPT-4.1 nano model now outperforms the older GPT-4o at 25× lower cost. The benchmark also includes a “HealthBench Hard” subset of 1,000 difficult examples and tracks worst-of-n reliability curves, showing room for further gains.

https://datascience.nih.gov/artificial-i.brief: NIH reports that it makes a wealth of biomedical data available to research communities. It aims to make these data “findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable, or FAIR” and usable with AI/ML applications. NIH notes that its unique data types, electronic health records, omics, imaging, disease-specific data, create opportunities for novel AI/ML approaches. The agency also emphasizes establishing partnerships and providing policies, guidelines, and best practices for investigators using AI in biomedical and behavioral research, and references Data Management Frameworks.

https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/.brief: The WHO report on ethics and governance of AI for health outlines the ethical challenges and risks of using AI in healthcare and presents six consensus principles to ensure AI benefits all countries. It was developed over eighteen months by experts in ethics, digital technology, law, human rights, and ministries of health. The guidance stresses that AI technologies, which can improve diagnosis, treatment, research, drug development, and support public health functions such as surveillance and outbreak response, must center ethics and human rights in their design, deployment, and use. It also offers recommendations to hold public and private stakeholders accountable and responsive to healthcare workers and affected communities.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/te.brief: The page lists the 1000 most-downloaded open medical models on the Hugging Face Hub, showing each model’s licence, download count, and release date, and it updates this information daily. It also mentions books by Stephen R. Jordan, including the “The Operating Discipline for AI Library™” series, now available on Amazon. Additionally, the page enumerates a range of AI audit and assessment services such as The AI Business Enablement Audit™, The AI Readiness & Performance Assessment™, The AI Risk & Governance Review™, The AI Efficiency & Process Optimization™, The AI IT Security Audit™, The AI IT Security Implementation & Strategy™, Secure by Design in the Age of AI™, Application Security in the Age of AI™, and The AI Lawyer.
